summary: Caribou National Forest summit: a 1942 silk-tent fire watch with shortwave radio on the 9,935-ft peak; no lookout structure in sources, nothing known about the site today.

staffing.status: 1942: fire watchman named Hauck (first name given as Frank and as Forrest), 12-hour vigil by shortwave radio

events.note: Fire watch from August 19, 1942: a watchman in a small silk tent on the summit, sheltering a two-way radio
Brush fire on Gardner range land off the Caribou Forest, reported from the Meade Peak lookout (item dated September 3, 1942)

evidence.supports: Summit elevation 9,935 feet; called the highest peak in southeast Idaho (1942 item)
evidence.quote: Meade Peak, elevation 9935 feet, about 4,000 feet above the old lake level which is now Bear River valley, has taken on new significance other than the fact that it is the highest peak in southeast Idaho.

evidence.supports: Watch from August 19 in a small silk tent sheltering a two-way radio, used by the fire watchman
evidence.quote: there has been since August 19 a small pyramidal silk tent sheltering a two-way radio and other instruments, used by the fire watchman assigned there

evidence.supports: Fire danger high: extreme fire hazard throughout the Caribou National Forest, the reason for the watch
evidence.quote: because of the extreme fire hazard now existing throughout the Caribou National Forest

evidence.supports: Watchman named Forrest Hauck keeps a 12-hour vigil and reports every 30 minutes
evidence.quote: Forrest Hauck, who maintains a 12 hour vigil from his lofty perch and reports fire and weather conditions on the short wave every 30 minutes, on the quarter after and to the hour.

evidence.supports: Hauck named as Frank in the brush-fire item
evidence.quote: A brush fire on the Gardner range land, off the Caribou Forest, was reported by Frank Hauck from the Meade Peak lookout Monday afternoon.

evidence.supports: Living quarters a tent and stove among evergreens in the south end of the basin
evidence.quote: Living quarters for the watchman, consisting of a tent and stove, sets in among the towering evergreens that grow in the south end of the basin

evidence.supports: Horseback trip up the Clear Creek trail takes about three hours
evidence.quote: The trip on horseback up the well-kept Clear creek trail takes about 3 hours

evidence.supports: Radio contact with Delphard Nicholls on Black Mountain and Lawrence Skinner on the Caribou Mountain lookout
evidence.quote: Radio communication is sustained between Mr. Hauck and Delphard Nicholls of Ovid, stationed on Black Mountain, and Lawrence Skinner of Gray's Lake on the Caribou Mountain look-out.

evidence.supports: Supervisor I.M. Varner in Pocatello can talk to each station
evidence.quote: Also each of these stations may talk Supervisor I.M. Varner in Pocatello.

evidence.supports: Fire helpers named; message relayed from Black Mountain to Etna, Wyoming, then by telephone to Ranger James Bruce
evidence.quote: Assisting in extinguishing the blaze were Eddie Wuthrich, W.R. Horning and officer Ross Parker of Montpelier.

evidence.supports: Message relayed from Black Mountain to Etna, Wyoming, then by telephone to Ranger James Bruce
evidence.quote: Mr. Hauck radioed to Black Mountain, which in turn radioed to Etna, Wyoming, from where the message was relayed by telephone to Ranger James Bruce.

evidence.supports: Approach: drive east into Georgetown Canyon from Georgetown
evidence.quote: From Georgetown, Idaho drive east into Georgetown Canyon.

evidence.supports: Follow the main track up the canyon to a clearing near the end, where the writers camped
evidence.quote: Just follow the main track up the canyon until you reach a clearing near the end with a fire ring of white rocks. We camped here.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1942 items reprinted on Forest Lookouts give Frank Hauck in the brush-fire item and Forrest Hauck in the vigil item. The story uses the surname only.

notes_for_editor: Only a 1942 newspaper account (reprinted on Forest Lookouts) describes the summit watch; no structure, build date, end of watch or fate is documented. Elevation 9,935 ft (about 3,028 m) is from the 1942 item and is not in facts; elevation_m stays null. Brief status, access and kind left as they are; no source supports changing them. NHLR and FFLOS caches have no Meade Peak entry. The second WebSearch found no new lookout history. The Rocky Mountain Summits page is a climbing report; the access note is its route, not a Forest Service rule.
